script.opening: "I’ve had this awful tummy bug for four days — diarrhoea and being sick — and I can hardly keep anything down. I feel weak and a bit dizzy when I stand. The nurse did a blood test and said my kidneys aren’t happy. I’ve been taking ibuprofen for the aches. Should I be worried?"

facts.text: Started 4 days ago after her grandson had the same. Watery diarrhoea 5–6 times a day, no blood. Vomiting 2–3 times a day, "even water comes back sometimes". Only managing small sips. Mild crampy tummy ache; no constant severe pain.
If asked: "I’ve hardly been to the toilet to wee — once this morning, dark like tea." Mouth very dry.

Weak and washed out. Dizzy and "grey" when she stands up; held onto the furniture this morning but didn’t fall or faint. Not muddled. No breathlessness, no chest pain. Felt hot yesterday; no thermometer. No rigors.
Has a glucose meter but "hasn’t bothered" this week. No ketone meter. Hasn’t been eating much at all. Not breathless or smelling of pear drops that she knows of.

Ramipril 10 mg for blood pressure, metformin 1 g twice daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg ("the sugar tablet that makes you wee"), atorvastatin. Has kept taking them all "because you’re not supposed to stop". Bought ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for 4 days for aches. No allergies. Nobody has ever mentioned "sick-day rules".
Diabetes for 8 years, blood pressure for 15. Told years ago her kidneys were "a little bit tired". No heart failure.
Widow, lives alone in a bungalow. Daughter, Karen, lives 20 minutes away and has a car — "she’d take me anywhere if needed". Retired school cook. Non-smoker, no alcohol.

Polite, tired, a bit vague. You don’t link the tablets to the kidneys and are surprised by it. If hospital is suggested, be reluctant at first ("I was hoping to stay at home") but agree if the reason is explained clearly. If the doctor asks you to say back the plan, do so.

ice.ideas: "It’s just a tummy bug. I don’t understand why my kidneys would be involved."
ice.concerns: "That my kidneys are packing up — my sister ended up on dialysis." Also quietly worried about going into hospital and catching something.
ice.expectations: "Something to stop the sickness, and to be told if I should worry." Hoping to stay at home.

cues: "I’ve been taking ibuprofen for the aches" — the NSAID on top of ramipril and dehydration.
"Dizzy when I stand" and "hardly been to the toilet" — significant dehydration.
"My sister ended up on dialysis" (if worries are explored) — the fear behind "should I be worried?".

checkpoints.text: Recognises pre-renal ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY from a dehydrating illness on an ACE inhibitor/ARB + NSAID — the classic ACEi/ARB + NSAID + intercurrent-illness/dehydration triad

Assesses severity, hydration and RED FLAGS — creatinine rise against baseline (NICE NG148 staging) and potassium, urine dipstick, blood ketones (SGLT2 inhibitor), postural dizziness (postural BP face to face), reduced urine output/anuria, confusion, fluid overload, hyperkalaemia risk, sepsis, inability to keep fluids down

Institutes SICK-DAY RULES — temporarily holds ACEi/ARB (ramipril), NSAID (ibuprofen), SGLT2 inhibitor (also DKA risk), metformin (accumulation/lactic acidosis), and diuretics — explaining when to restart (Think Kidneys 2018: after 24–48 hours of normal eating and drinking; ramipril only after renal recovery on a recheck)

Manages hydration (oral rehydration if tolerating) and decides DISPOSITION — admitting for IV fluids/monitoring if unable to maintain fluids, severe AKI, hyperkalaemia, anuria, confusion or sepsis — here same-day hospital assessment, given vomiting, postural dizziness, diabetes and the SGLT2 inhibitor
Arranges to RECHECK U&E/renal function within a few days (and review restarting medications), and gives clear FUTURE SICK-DAY guidance (and avoiding routine NSAIDs in at-risk patients)
Explains the link between the illness, the tablets/ibuprofen and the kidney result in accessible terms, addressing "should I be worried?" proportionately
Checks understanding of the medication holds and the recheck plan, and supports the patient through the illness

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review/admission (can’t keep fluids, reduced urine, drowsiness/confusion, palpitations), the recheck and medication-restart plan, and future sick-day rules — active AKI management, not leaving her on the offending drugs

worked.txt: "Yes, but it’s manageable — let me explain what’s happened. The tummy bug has dried you out, and two of your tablets — the ramipril for blood pressure and the ibuprofen — strain the kidneys when you’re dehydrated. Together they’ve given you a kidney ‘wobble’ we call acute kidney injury. It usually recovers."

"A few checks: are you passing much less urine? Any dizziness on standing, palpitations, drowsiness or confusion? Can you keep any fluids down at all? … Those tell me whether we can sort this at home or you need a drip in hospital."

"The key step now: STOP the ibuprofen completely, and pause the ramipril, your metformin and the SGLT2 diabetes tablet while you’re unwell and not eating/drinking properly — they can build up or strain the kidneys when you’re dry. We restart them once you’ve been eating and drinking normally for a day or two — and the ramipril only once a blood test shows your kidneys have recovered."

"Sip fluids little and often — rehydration sachets are ideal. If you genuinely can’t keep anything down, are passing very little urine, or feel really unwell, you’ll need hospital for a drip. With the vomiting, the dizziness on standing, your diabetes and that SGLT2 tablet, I don’t think home is safe today: I’d like you assessed in hospital today for fluids, a repeat kidney and potassium test and a ketone check."

"After the hospital check, I’ll arrange a repeat kidney blood test in a few days to be sure it’s recovering and to restart your tablets safely. And for the future: any time you get a bad D&V bug, pause those same tablets and let us know — I’ll give you a sick-day list."

"Come back urgently — or call 999 — if you stop passing urine, become drowsy or confused, get palpitations or chest symptoms, or can’t keep fluids down. Otherwise, fluids, hold those tablets, and we’ll recheck."

f.learning: A rise in creatinine after a DEHYDRATING illness (diarrhoea/vomiting, poor intake) in a patient on an ACE INHIBITOR/ARB and an NSAID is the classic recipe for pre-renal ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY — the "triad" of ACEi/ARB + NSAID + intercurrent illness/dehydration — a common, often reversible, but dangerous problem. Assess severity (creatinine rise against baseline — NICE NG148: 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours or 50% or more within 7 days — and the potassium, with a urine dipstick and, on an SGLT2 inhibitor, blood ketones per MHRA March 2020), hydration (postural dizziness and reduced URINE output/anuria by history; postural BP and dry mucosa need a face-to-face check) and RED FLAGS (confusion/drowsiness, fluid overload, features/risk of HYPERKALAEMIA — the dangerous electrolyte needing urgent K+/ECG — sepsis, and inability to keep fluids down), which determine home versus admission. The key examinable action is SICK-DAY RULES: temporarily STOP the medications that worsen AKI or accumulate during acute illness — ACEi/ARB, NSAID (stop and avoid), SGLT2 inhibitor (also euglycaemic DKA risk when unwell), metformin (accumulation/lactic acidosis risk in AKI) and diuretics — explaining to resume after 24–48 hours of eating and drinking normally (Think Kidneys 2018), with the ACE inhibitor restarted only once renal function has recovered. Manage hydration with oral rehydration if tolerated, but ADMIT for IV fluids/monitoring if the patient cannot keep fluids down or has severe AKI, hyperkalaemia, anuria, confusion or sepsis — and an older, diabetic patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor who is vomiting with postural dizziness needs same-day hospital assessment rather than a trial at home. Arrange to RECHECK U&E within a few days (and review restarting medications), and give clear FUTURE SICK-DAY guidance — pausing the listed drugs and seeking advice during any dehydrating illness, ideally on a sick-day card — while avoiding routine NSAIDs in at-risk patients. The hidden agenda is the patient not connecting her tablets/ibuprofen to the result; explain the link, institute the holds, decide disposition safely, recheck, and equip her for the future — not ignore the AKI or leave her on the offending drugs.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG148 (acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, 2019) · [2] Think Kidneys (NHS England programme) sick day guidance (2018) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update March 2020 (SGLT2 inhibitors: monitor ketones in blood during treatment interruption for surgical procedures or acute serious medical illness) · [4] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults, updated) · [5] NICE NG253 (suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over, 2025) · [6] BNF monographs for ramipril, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors and ibuprofen
knowledge.summary: Four days of diarrhoea and vomiting, barely keeping fluids down, dizziness on standing and a rise in creatinine, in a 72-year-old on ramipril, metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor and ibuprofen: this is acute kidney injury from volume depletion made worse by her medicines. Stop the ibuprofen, pause the ramipril, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor, and — because she cannot keep fluids down, is older, diabetic and on an SGLT2 inhibitor — arrange same-day hospital assessment rather than a trial at home. Then make sure the held drugs are restarted safely and she has a sick-day plan.

points.t: NICE NG148 [1] uses a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a 50% or greater rise within the past 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. Compare with her previous result — without a baseline you cannot stage it.

NICE NG148 [1] risk factors present here: age 65 or over, diabetes, hypovolaemia from diarrhoea and vomiting, and nephrotoxic or risk drugs (ACE inhibitor, NSAID). An ACE inhibitor or ARB with an NSAID during a dehydrating illness is a classic route to AKI [1][2].

Ask about urine output, postural dizziness, drowsiness or confusion, breathlessness, palpitations, fever and whether any fluid stays down. Check potassium on the result. Consider sepsis (NICE NG253 [5]). NICE NG148 [1]: urine dipstick for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose in everyone with suspected AKI.

She cannot keep fluids down, is 72, has postural symptoms, diabetes and an SGLT2 inhibitor: she needs same-day hospital assessment for IV fluids, repeat U&E and potassium, ketones and monitoring. Home management is reserved for a well patient with mild AKI who can drink, with a recheck within 48 hours. Hyperkalaemia, anuria, confusion or signs of sepsis mean emergency admission.

Think Kidneys [2]: during a dehydrating illness temporarily stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors and sulfonylureas, and restart after 24–48 hours of eating and drinking normally. NICE NG148 [1]: stop nephrotoxic drugs in AKI and review them before restarting. After AKI, restart the ramipril only once kidney function has recovered.

MHRA March 2020 [3]: diabetic ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose on an SGLT2 inhibitor. Interrupt treatment in acute serious illness, check blood ketones, and restart only when ketones are normal and she is stable.
Metformin accumulates when kidney function falls, raising the risk of lactic acidosis. Pause during the illness; restart when eGFR has recovered, with dose adjusted to eGFR per BNF [6].

Recheck U&E before restarting held drugs; avoid NSAIDs in future (paracetamol instead); give a written sick-day card; code the AKI and monitor for CKD afterwards [1]. The ramipril must not be dropped by accident — restarting is as important as stopping.

model.text: Hello Mrs Drake, I’m Dr Morgan. Can you hear and see me all right? I’m sorry you’ve been so unwell. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens with empathy

model.text: I’ve had this awful tummy bug for four days — diarrhoea and being sick — and I can hardly keep anything down. I feel weak and a bit dizzy when I stand. The nurse did a blood test and said my kidneys aren’t happy. I’ve been taking ibuprofen for the aches. Should I be worried?
That’s a fair question and I’ll answer it honestly. I have your result in front of me. Can I ask a few quick questions first, then explain what it means and what we need to do today?
model.why: Sets an agenda and signals urgency without alarm

model.text: Yes, please.
Over the last day, how much have you managed to keep down? And how often are you passing water — less than usual?
model.why: Assesses oral intake and urine output

model.text: Only little sips, and sometimes they come back up. I’ve hardly been to the toilet.
When you stand, do you feel faint or need to hold on? Have you felt drowsy or muddled, had a racing or irregular heartbeat, any breathlessness, or a temperature or shivers?
model.why: Screens postural hypovolaemia, confusion, hyperkalaemia symptoms, sepsis

model.text: Dizzy when I stand, yes. Not muddled, I don’t think.
Any blood in the diarrhoea or vomit, or bad tummy pain? And do you have a way of checking your sugar or ketones at home?
model.why: Screens complications and SGLT2-related ketoacidosis risk

model.text: No blood. I don’t check anything at home.
And your tablets — are you still taking the ramipril, the metformin and the diabetes tablet that makes you pass sugar in the urine, alongside the ibuprofen?
model.why: Confirms each risk drug is still being taken

model.text: Yes, I’ve been trying to keep them all down.
What have you been thinking this blood test means?
I thought it was just the bug. I didn’t know why my kidneys would be involved. I’d hoped you’d give me something to stop the sickness.

It makes complete sense to think it’s just the bug. What’s happened is that the bug has dried you out, and some tablets — the ramipril and the ibuprofen especially — make it harder for dry kidneys to keep working. Together they’ve caused what we call an acute kidney injury. It’s common, and it usually recovers when the fluids and tablets are sorted out.
model.why: Explains the illness–drug link in plain words

model.text: So should I be worried?

I’m concerned enough that I want you seen in hospital today. You can’t keep fluids down, you’re dizzy when you stand and passing very little urine. At this stage you need a drip, repeat blood tests including your potassium, and a check for a build-up of acid in the blood that your diabetes tablet can cause even when the sugar isn’t high. I can’t check any of that safely over video.
model.why: Clear same-day hospital disposition with reasons

model.text: Hospital? I was hoping to stay at home.

I understand — nobody wants to go in. If you could drink and were only mildly affected, we’d manage it at home with a recheck in a day or two. But with this much fluid loss, I’d be taking a risk with your kidneys to keep you home. Most people with this recover well once they’re rehydrated. Is that all right with you?
model.why: Acknowledges reluctance, explains the threshold, seeks agreement

model.text: If you think it’s needed. Yes.

Thank you. Until you’re seen, stop the ibuprofen completely, and don’t take the ramipril, the metformin or the SGLT2 tablet. Keep sipping fluids if you can. I’ll speak to the medical team at the hospital now and send them a letter with your results and the tablets we’ve stopped. Can someone take you, or shall we arrange transport?
model.why: Sick-day holds, handover to the acute team, practical transport

model.text: I’ll sort out getting there.

When you’re better, the hospital or I will recheck your kidney test before restarting the tablets — they’re important for your blood pressure and diabetes, so we won’t just leave them off. For aches in future, use paracetamol rather than ibuprofen. And I’ll give you a sick-day card: whenever you have vomiting, diarrhoea or can’t eat and drink, pause these tablets and ring us.
model.why: Restart plan, NSAID avoidance, future sick-day rules (Think Kidneys)

model.text: I never knew the tablets could do that.
Could you tell me back which tablets you’re stopping and what happens next?
Stop the ibuprofen, the ramipril, the metformin and the sugar tablet. Go to the hospital today. Kidney test before restarting.

Exactly. If before you get there you become drowsy or confused, faint, feel your heart racing or fluttering, or become breathless, call 999. I’ll follow up after you’re discharged to restart your tablets safely. Is there anything else worrying you?
model.why: Specific 999 triggers and a defined follow-up

model.text: No. Thank you for explaining it — I’d never have connected it.

social.t: Older patients often resist admission. Explain the specific reason and what would make home management safe, so the decision is shared rather than imposed.
Bought ibuprofen is easily missed. Ask about over-the-counter and pharmacy medicines at every review; community pharmacists can reinforce avoidance.

legal.t: She has capacity to accept or decline admission. If she declines, explain the risks clearly, document the discussion, agree a close safety net and a recheck, and review early.

professional.t: Tell the acute team which drugs were paused and why. After discharge, reconcile the list so held drugs are restarted appropriately (NICE NG148: review nephrotoxic drugs after AKI).
Record the AKI episode and arrange follow-up of kidney function, since AKI raises the risk of later CKD (NICE NG148).

community.t: Think Kidneys sick-day guidance cards; community pharmacy medicines review; Kidney Care UK patient information.

redFlags: Cannot keep fluids down, passing very little urine, postural dizziness — same-day hospital assessment
Drowsiness, confusion, palpitations, breathlessness — possible hyperkalaemia, sepsis or ketoacidosis: 999
Fever, rigors or blood in stool — sepsis or complicated gastroenteritis
psychosocial: How she will get to hospital
Understanding of which tablets to pause
ice: Idea: it’s just the tummy bug
Concern: whether the kidney result is serious
Expectation: something to stop the sickness

playbook.diagnosis: Acute kidney injury (NICE NG148) from volume depletion after 4 days of diarrhoea and vomiting, worsened by ramipril and ibuprofen, in a 72-year-old with type 2 diabetes on metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Unable to maintain oral intake, with postural symptoms: same-day hospital assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The bug has dried you out, and some of your tablets make it harder for dry kidneys to cope. Together they’ve strained your kidneys. It usually recovers once you’re rehydrated and the tablets are paused.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was just the bug — and the bug started it. But with your tablets, it’s now affecting your kidneys, which is why we act today.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge her reluctance; explain the threshold for home care; confirm how she will get there.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment with verbal and written handover
Stop ibuprofen; pause ramipril, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor (Think Kidneys; MHRA March 2020)
Restart after recovery and a repeat U&E; ramipril only once kidney function has recovered
Future: paracetamol not NSAIDs; written sick-day card; follow-up of kidney function after AKI
safetyNet: Drowsy, confused, faint, palpitations or breathless before reaching hospital — 999
GP review after discharge to reconcile and restart medicines

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating the tummy bug and missing the kidneys, or by recognising the AKI and still keeping an older patient at home who cannot drink.

items.fail: Antiemetic and ‘push fluids’ with no medicine changes.
items.why: Continuing ramipril and ibuprofen during dehydration worsens AKI.
items.fix: Stop the NSAID and pause the ACE inhibitor, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor.

items.fail: Managing at home when she cannot keep fluids down.
items.why: She is 72, diabetic, on an SGLT2 inhibitor, with postural symptoms and AKI.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment with a handover.

items.fail: Forgetting ketoacidosis on the SGLT2 inhibitor.
items.why: MHRA March 2020: ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose.
items.fix: Pause it and make sure ketones are checked.

items.why: Held ACE inhibitors are often never restarted.
items.fix: Recheck U&E and restart deliberately; reconcile medicines after discharge.

items.fail: Insisting on admission without explaining why.
items.why: She wanted to stay home; an unexplained order undermines trust.
items.fix: Give the specific reasons and what would have made home safe.

items.fail: Claiming to assess hydration over video.
items.why: Postural BP, mucosa and urine output cannot be examined remotely.
items.fix: Use history, name the limits, and send her for assessment.

items.why: The next bug will cause the same injury.
items.fix: Written sick-day card, paracetamol not NSAIDs, and a clear ‘pause and ring us’ rule.

avoid.instead: “You can’t keep fluids down and your kidneys are struggling — you need a drip in hospital today.”

SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the illness–drug link in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: So should I be worried?

I’m concerned enough that I want you seen in hospital today. You can’t keep fluids down, you’re dizzy when you stand and passing very little urine. At this stage you need a drip, repeat blood tests including your potassium, and a check for a build-up of acid in the blood that your diabetes tablet can cause even when the sugar isn’t high. I can’t check any of that safely over video.
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear same-day hospital disposition with reasons

SCA_MODELS.text: Hospital? I was hoping to stay at home.

I understand — nobody wants to go in. If you could drink and were only mildly affected, we’d manage it at home with a recheck in a day or two. But with this much fluid loss, I’d be taking a risk with your kidneys to keep you home. Most people with this recover well once they’re rehydrated. Is that all right with you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges reluctance, explains the threshold, seeks agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: If you think it’s needed. Yes.

Thank you. Until you’re seen, stop the ibuprofen completely, and don’t take the ramipril, the metformin or the SGLT2 tablet. Keep sipping fluids if you can. I’ll speak to the medical team at the hospital now and send them a letter with your results and the tablets we’ve stopped. Can someone take you, or shall we arrange transport?
SCA_MODELS.why: Sick-day holds, handover to the acute team, practical transport

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll sort out getting there.

When you’re better, the hospital or I will recheck your kidney test before restarting the tablets — they’re important for your blood pressure and diabetes, so we won’t just leave them off. For aches in future, use paracetamol rather than ibuprofen. And I’ll give you a sick-day card: whenever you have vomiting, diarrhoea or can’t eat and drink, pause these tablets and ring us.
SCA_MODELS.why: Restart plan, NSAID avoidance, future sick-day rules (Think Kidneys)

SCA_MODELS.text: I never knew the tablets could do that.
Could you tell me back which tablets you’re stopping and what happens next?
Stop the ibuprofen, the ramipril, the metformin and the sugar tablet. Go to the hospital today. Kidney test before restarting.

Exactly. If before you get there you become drowsy or confused, faint, feel your heart racing or fluttering, or become breathless, call 999. I’ll follow up after you’re discharged to restart your tablets safely. Is there anything else worrying you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific 999 triggers and a defined follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you for explaining it — I’d never have connected it.

SCA_STEM.recent: 4 days of diarrhoea and vomiting. Blood test taken by the practice nurse: creatinine risen from her previous result — acute kidney injury flagged. Check potassium and the previous baseline on the record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation. “A blood test says my kidneys are off — should I be worried?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG148 (acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, 2019) · [2] Think Kidneys (NHS England programme) sick day guidance (2018) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update March 2020 (SGLT2 inhibitors: monitor ketones in blood during treatment interruption for surgical procedures or acute serious medical illness) · [4] NICE NG28 (type 2 diabetes in adults, updated) · [5] NICE NG253 (suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over, 2025) · [6] BNF monographs for ramipril, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors and ibuprofen
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Four days of diarrhoea and vomiting, barely keeping fluids down, dizziness on standing and a rise in creatinine, in a 72-year-old on ramipril, metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor and ibuprofen: this is acute kidney injury from volume depletion made worse by her medicines. Stop the ibuprofen, pause the ramipril, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor, and — because she cannot keep fluids down, is older, diabetic and on an SGLT2 inhibitor — arrange same-day hospital assessment rather than a trial at home. Then make sure the held drugs are restarted safely and she has a sick-day plan.

points.t: NICE NG148 [1] uses a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a 50% or greater rise within the past 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. Compare with her previous result — without a baseline you cannot stage it.

NICE NG148 [1] risk factors present here: age 65 or over, diabetes, hypovolaemia from diarrhoea and vomiting, and nephrotoxic or risk drugs (ACE inhibitor, NSAID). An ACE inhibitor or ARB with an NSAID during a dehydrating illness is a classic route to AKI [1][2].

Ask about urine output, postural dizziness, drowsiness or confusion, breathlessness, palpitations, fever and whether any fluid stays down. Check potassium on the result. Consider sepsis (NICE NG253 [5]). NICE NG148 [1]: urine dipstick for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose in everyone with suspected AKI.

She cannot keep fluids down, is 72, has postural symptoms, diabetes and an SGLT2 inhibitor: she needs same-day hospital assessment for IV fluids, repeat U&E and potassium, ketones and monitoring. Home management is reserved for a well patient with mild AKI who can drink, with a recheck within 48 hours. Hyperkalaemia, anuria, confusion or signs of sepsis mean emergency admission.

Think Kidneys [2]: during a dehydrating illness temporarily stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors and sulfonylureas, and restart after 24–48 hours of eating and drinking normally. NICE NG148 [1]: stop nephrotoxic drugs in AKI and review them before restarting. After AKI, restart the ramipril only once kidney function has recovered.

MHRA March 2020 [3]: diabetic ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose on an SGLT2 inhibitor. Interrupt treatment in acute serious illness, check blood ketones, and restart only when ketones are normal and she is stable.
Metformin accumulates when kidney function falls, raising the risk of lactic acidosis. Pause during the illness; restart when eGFR has recovered, with dose adjusted to eGFR per BNF [6].

Recheck U&E before restarting held drugs; avoid NSAIDs in future (paracetamol instead); give a written sick-day card; code the AKI and monitor for CKD afterwards [1]. The ramipril must not be dropped by accident — restarting is as important as stopping.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question after checking the video link; let her describe the illness and ask ‘should I be worried?’
Explored her wish to stay home and how she will get to hospital; checked what she thought the result meant.
Picked up ‘hardly keep anything down’, ‘dizzy when I stand’ and ibuprofen use as the key cues.
Idea: just the bug. Concern: whether it’s serious. Expectation: something to stop the sickness.
Checked the previous creatinine and potassium on the record; stated what video cannot assess; hospital to do U&E, ketones, urine dip, obs.
Pre-renal AKI from volume depletion with ACE inhibitor and NSAID; considered sepsis, ketoacidosis on SGLT2 inhibitor and hyperkalaemia.
Screened urine output, postural symptoms, confusion, palpitations, breathlessness, fever, blood in stool.
AKI (NICE NG148 criteria) in a 72-year-old with diabetes, unable to maintain oral fluids.
Same-day hospital assessment with handover; stop ibuprofen; pause ramipril, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor (Think Kidneys; MHRA 2020).
Planned restart after recheck so ramipril and diabetes treatment are not lost; NSAID avoidance; sick-day card.
999 triggers before arrival; teach-back of the holds; GP follow-up after discharge.

social.t: Older patients often resist admission. Explain the specific reason and what would make home management safe, so the decision is shared rather than imposed.
Bought ibuprofen is easily missed. Ask about over-the-counter and pharmacy medicines at every review; community pharmacists can reinforce avoidance.

legal.t: She has capacity to accept or decline admission. If she declines, explain the risks clearly, document the discussion, agree a close safety net and a recheck, and review early.

professional.t: Tell the acute team which drugs were paused and why. After discharge, reconcile the list so held drugs are restarted appropriately (NICE NG148: review nephrotoxic drugs after AKI).
Record the AKI episode and arrange follow-up of kidney function, since AKI raises the risk of later CKD (NICE NG148).

community.t: Think Kidneys sick-day guidance cards; community pharmacy medicines review; Kidney Care UK patient information.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating the tummy bug and missing the kidneys, or by recognising the AKI and still keeping an older patient at home who cannot drink.

items.fail: Antiemetic and ‘push fluids’ with no medicine changes.
items.why: Continuing ramipril and ibuprofen during dehydration worsens AKI.
items.fix: Stop the NSAID and pause the ACE inhibitor, metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor.

items.fail: Managing at home when she cannot keep fluids down.
items.why: She is 72, diabetic, on an SGLT2 inhibitor, with postural symptoms and AKI.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment with a handover.

items.fail: Forgetting ketoacidosis on the SGLT2 inhibitor.
items.why: MHRA March 2020: ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose.
items.fix: Pause it and make sure ketones are checked.

items.why: Held ACE inhibitors are often never restarted.
items.fix: Recheck U&E and restart deliberately; reconcile medicines after discharge.

items.fail: Insisting on admission without explaining why.
items.why: She wanted to stay home; an unexplained order undermines trust.
items.fix: Give the specific reasons and what would have made home safe.

items.fail: Claiming to assess hydration over video.
items.why: Postural BP, mucosa and urine output cannot be examined remotely.
items.fix: Use history, name the limits, and send her for assessment.

items.why: The next bug will cause the same injury.
items.fix: Written sick-day card, paracetamol not NSAIDs, and a clear ‘pause and ring us’ rule.
